The program currently collects and publishes financial data for the manufacturing, mining, wholesale trade, retail trade, information, and professional and technical services (except legal) sectors. prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Quarterly Financial Report (QFR)
Description: The Quarterly Financial Report (QFR) program collects and publishes quarterly aggregate statistics on the financial results and position of U.S. corporations. The program currently collects and publishes financial data for the manufacturing, mining, wholesale trade, retail trade, information, and professional and technical services (except legal) sectors. The survey is a principal economic indicator that provides financial data essential to calculation of key U.S. government measures of national economic performance. Several U.S. Census Bureau reports, including Corporate Profits, Retail Trade, and Manufacturing, Mining, and Wholesale Trade, are produced using these data.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Quarterly Financial Report (QFR): Dataset Research Report

## Summary

Your description is mostly accurate. Much of it is copied almost word for word from the Census Bureau's own paperwork filed with the Office of Management and Budget (OMB). There is one clear error and a few gaps:

1. **"Corporate Profits" is not a Census Bureau report.** It is a Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) estimate within the National Income and Product Accounts (NIPA), and QFR data feed into it. "Retail Trade" and "Manufacturing, Mining, and Wholesale Trade" are not separate Census reports built from QFR data. They are the QFR's own two quarterly press releases.
2. **The survey does not cover all U.S. corporations.** Only manufacturers with $5 million or more in domestic assets are in scope. Mining, wholesale, retail and selected service corporations must have $50 million or more.
3. **The sector names are slightly loose.** The services sector is professional, *scientific*, and technical services (NAICS 541), excluding legal services (5411). "Information" means NAICS 512–513 and 516–519. Retail covers NAICS 441, 444–445, 449 and 455–459.
4. **Missing points:** the program is one of the oldest continuous federal economic series (data since 1947), and its legal authority expires on **September 30, 2030** unless Congress renews it.

---

## 1. Publisher and contacts
- **Publisher:** U.S. Census Bureau (Department of Commerce), economic programs. The QFR is one of the Census Bureau's Principal Federal Economic Indicators, which are listed in its Economic Briefing Room calendar.
- **Contact:** The Manufacturing Surveys Statistical Methods Branch handles methodology questions (301‑763‑7630). The press release lists a QFR email (the text I found was garbled; it is probably csd.qfr@census.gov, so verify it on the release).
- **Website:** https://www.census.gov/econ/qfr/
- **OMB control number:** 0607‑0432. The current approval runs through **August 31, 2027**.

## 2. Legal authority
- **13 U.S.C. § 91** authorizes the survey and *requires* that financial statistics on business operations be collected and published every quarter.
- **13 U.S.C. § 9** makes responses confidential and limits their use to statistics. No published figure may identify a business.
- **Response is mandatory** for selected companies.
- **Laws that transferred and renewed the program:**
  - **P.L. 97‑454** (enacted January 1983) moved the QFR from the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) to the Secretary of Commerce. This is why some sources say 1982 and others 1983.
  - **P.L. 109‑79** (2005) renewed it through 2015.
  - **P.L. 114‑72** (the QFR Reauthorization Act, H.R. 3116) renewed it through **September 30, 2030** (see House Report 114‑237).
- Submitted data are also protected under the Federal Cybersecurity Enhancement Act of 2015, which allows screening of the systems that transmit the data.
- **Policy note:** Because the authority expires on a set date, the program's survival depends on Congress renewing it before September 2030. That is the main point where advocacy matters.

## 3. History

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 1938–41 | The FTC publishes a forerunner, the "Quarterly Industrial Financial Report Series" |
| WWII | Data collection rests with the Office of Price Administration, according to Census's "About" page. A Census webinar instead says the FTC simply stopped the program. Sources differ here. |
| 1946 | An executive order returns the program to the FTC. After the war it is run jointly by the FTC and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). |
| Oct 31, 1947 | The first published quarter (1Q 1947) |
| 1951 | Renamed "Quarterly Financial Report" |
| 1971 | The FTC takes sole responsibility |
| 4Q 1974 | First expansion of coverage since 1947 |
| 4Q 1982 | Transferred to the Census Bureau |
| 1Q 1987 | First seasonally adjusted figures |
| 4Q 2001 | Switch from the older SIC industry codes to NAICS (4Q 2000–1Q 2001 restated) |
| 4Q 2010 | Information and professional/scientific/technical services added; the survey now covers about 37% of GDP. A new method for estimating missing responses is introduced. |
| 1Q 2016 | Retail trade released at the same time as the other sectors |
| 4Q 2024 | Estimates move to 2022 NAICS (a break in the series) |
| Oct–Nov 2025 | A lapse in federal funding disrupted Census indicators, and Census issued a recovery plan. I could not confirm whether the 3Q 2025 QFR release came out on its scheduled date. |
| 2Q 2026 (released Sept 8, 2026) | New disclosure-avoidance protections begin under Commerce order DAO 216‑26 (details below) |

## 4. Coverage and content
- **What it covers:** U.S. corporations in mining (NAICS 211–213), manufacturing (311–339), wholesale (423–425), retail (selected industries listed above), information (512–513, 516–519) and professional, scientific and technical services except legal (541 minus 5411), subject to the asset thresholds above.
- **What it contains:** estimated income statements and retained earnings, balance sheets, and financial and operating ratios (for example, after-tax return on sales and on equity). Figures are broken out by industry and, for manufacturing, by asset size.
- **Seasonal adjustment** (using the X‑13ARIMA‑SEATS program) applies only to a few headline series. Sales and after-tax income are adjusted for total, durable and nondurable manufacturing and for professional and technical services. Only sales are adjusted for retail, information and wholesale. Everything else is unadjusted.
- **Timing:** about 75 days after the end of the first three quarters and about 90 days after the fourth. Companies report on their own fiscal quarters, which are mapped to calendar quarters (retail's quarters are shifted one month later).
- **Latest release I found:** 2Q 2026, issued September 8, 2026. Seasonally adjusted after-tax profits were $359.4 billion for manufacturing and $112.3 billion for large retailers. The next release is scheduled for **December 7, 2026**.

## 5. Methodology
- **Sample source:** a list built each year from IRS records of corporations that file Form 1120.
- **Sample design:** corporations above industry-specific asset cutoffs (roughly $250 million and up) are always included. Smaller firms are drawn at random within industry and asset-size groups. Each group of smaller firms stays in the sample for 8 quarters, and one-eighth of them is replaced each quarter.
- **Forms:**
  - QFR‑200(MT): long form for manufacturing, mining and trade, about 3.0 hours.
  - QFR‑201(MG): short form for small and mid-size manufacturers, about 1.2 hours.
  - QFR‑300(S): services, about 3.0 hours.
  - Collection is by mail and online (the Centurion system).
- **Respondent burden:** about 34,288 responses and 82,898 hours a year (2024 approval), with no cost to respondents beyond their time.
- **Missing responses:** since 4Q 2010, values are filled in statistically (mainly with a ratio method that uses each company's earlier reports and similar companies). Unusual values are screened out of the inputs. Response rates and the share of each total that was filled in are published with every release.
- **Revisions:** the prior quarter is revised, and seasonally adjusted history is revised every quarter.

## 6. Users and uses
- **BEA:** a main source for current quarterly estimates of corporate profits, taxes and dividends, which go into Gross Domestic Income (GDI) and the national accounts.
- **Federal Reserve Board:** a building block of the Financial Accounts (formerly Flow of Funds) and its only source of consolidated financial data on nonfinancial corporations.
- **Other government users:**
  - Treasury's Office of Tax Analysis and the Joint Committee on Taxation: estimating the effects of tax law and answering congressional questions.
  - Small Business Administration: comparing small and large firms.
  - FTC: studying ownership concentration in manufacturing.
  - Council of Economic Advisers and Bureau of Land Management.
- **Private and academic users:** universities, financial analysts, unions, trade associations, banks, public libraries, and U.S. and foreign corporations. Common uses are analyzing debt, liquidity and profitability, investment evaluation, and business-cycle research. The QFR's size-class data are a classic source for comparing small and large firms.

## 7. Public benefits
- It is the only timely, regular source of aggregated balance sheets and income statements for U.S. corporations by industry, and it includes privately held mid-size companies that file nothing with the SEC.
- It supports the accuracy of GDP and GDI, the Fed's monitoring of financial stability, and tax policy.
- It is free, and the series runs back to 1947.

## 8. Access and formats
- Press releases and full publications (PDF and Excel), plus historical files: https://www.census.gov/econ/qfr/historic.html. The summary tables are large, about 128 MB per quarter.
- Time Series/Trend Charts tool, which includes sampling-error measures: https://www.census.gov/econ/currentdata/?programCode=QFR
- **Census Data API:** `api.census.gov/data/timeseries/eits/qfr` (requires a free API key).
- **FRED/ALFRED** (St. Louis Fed) carries QFR series with past versions of the data preserved, e.g. QFR115MFGUSNO.

## 9. Caveats for data scientists
- **Breaks in the series:** SIC to NAICS (2001), the 2010 services expansion and new method for missing responses, and 2022 NAICS starting 4Q 2024. Retail's release format changed in 2016.
- The 2026 disclosure-avoidance change may suppress or alter some cells compared with earlier releases.
- Each company is assigned to a single industry, so large conglomerates can blur industry totals.
- Rotating the sample adds "noise" (Census publishes an FAQ on this). Check the standard errors and relative standard errors before reading small changes as real.
- Size thresholds mean small non-manufacturers are excluded. Figures are not adjusted for inflation.

## 10. Notes for preservationists
- The historical publications are scattered PDFs and very large Excel files. Older FTC- and SEC-era volumes probably exist in FRASER, HathiTrust and federal depository libraries, but I did not confirm this.
- Worth archiving: the methodology PDF, the response-rate history, the seasonal factors, the OMB filings (forms and supporting statements), and past versions of the data (ALFRED holds some).
- Risks: the 2030 expiry of legal authority, funding lapses (as in 2025), and changes in disclosure rules.

**Not verified:** the full text of DAO 216‑26 (I ran out of searches) and the exact Census division that runs the program today.

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

# QFR Risk Assessment

The Quarterly Financial Report (QFR) is in better shape than many federal datasets. The law explicitly requires it, its funding is stable, and recent releases are on schedule. The main risks come from the Census Bureau as a whole: lost staff, political leadership, and a Commerce Department order that changed how QFR protects company confidentiality.

## Corrections to my earlier report
- **The 3Q 2025 release was late.** It came out December 15, 2025 instead of the scheduled December 8. The 43-day shutdown caused the delay ([Census 2025 calendar](https://www.census.gov/economic-indicators/calendar-listview-2025.html)).
- **I misdescribed the disclosure change.** From 4Q 2023 through 1Q 2026, QFR added random "noise" to published figures to protect individual companies. Starting with 2Q 2026, it went back to withholding sensitive cells ("suppression"), as required by Commerce order DAO 216‑26 ([QFR methodology](https://www.census.gov/econ/qfr/documents/QFR_Methodology.pdf); [Census Director's blog, Aug 2026](https://www.census.gov/newsroom/blogs/director/2026/08/understanding-the-new-disclosure-avoidance-policy.html)). I had called it new "protections."
- **Contact email confirmed:** csd.qfr@census.gov (on the survey form instructions).

---

### 1. Historical Data Availability
**Evidence**
- Press releases and publications for 2020–2026 are still listed, and historical files go back decades ([historical releases page](https://www.census.gov/econ/qfr/mmws/hist_releases.html)). The API and FRED/ALFRED copies are intact.
- The Census blog says DAO 216‑26 "applies only to new products going forward"; already-published products are not affected.
- **One caveat:** under the noise method, figures for the current and four prior quarters were perturbed. Revised back-quarters published under the new method will replace those noisy versions in current tables. That is a normal revision, not a removal, but archivists should keep the 4Q 2023–1Q 2026 versions as published.
- I found no reports of files being taken down.

**Rating: No Known Issue.**

### 2. Future Data Availability
**Evidence**
- **Moderate risk:** the 3Q 2025 release missed its scheduled date by one week because of the funding lapse ([Census recovery plan](https://www.census.gov/econ/indicators/census-pfei-recovery-2025-lapse-in-funding.pdf)).
- **No known issue:** every 2026 release came out on schedule (March 23, June 8, September 8), and the next is set for December 7, 2026 ([release schedule](https://www.census.gov/econ/qfr/release_schedule.html)). OMB approval of the survey (ICR 0607‑0432) is active through **August 31, 2027** ([reginfo.gov](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAViewICR?ref_nbr=202406-0607-001)). No release was skipped and there was no gap in the series.
- **Watch:** a Federal Register notice to renew OMB approval should appear around early 2027. A future shutdown could cause another delay.

**Rating: Moderate Risk (low end).** A strict reading of the rubric counts the missed date. The cause was outside the agency's control, and the schedule has fully recovered.

### 3. Data Quality
**Evidence**
- **Moderate risk:** suppression withholds cells. The Census blog says coarsening and suppression "can reduce the amount and detail of data published," and that the QFR "is affected." Fine industry-by-size cells could disappear. The one-week shutdown delay also briefly hurt timeliness.
- **No known issue:** the switch removes noise, which may make the numbers more accurate. Suppression is the method QFR used before 2023. Frequency and sector coverage are unchanged, and standard errors are still published.

**Rating: Moderate Risk.** The risk to detail is emerging, not confirmed. Users should compare suppressed cells in 2Q 2026 tables against earlier releases.

### 4. Statutory Context
**Evidence**
- 13 U.S.C. § 91 *requires* quarterly collection and publication of corporate financial statistics. P.L. 114‑72 reauthorizes it through September 30, 2030.
- The data are required for BEA's estimates of corporate profits and Gross Domestic Income, and for the Federal Reserve's Financial Accounts.
- No substitute exists. SEC filings cover only publicly traded firms, and IRS data arrive years later.
- **Caveat:** the authority expires in 2030 unless Congress renews it.

**Rating: No Known Issue.**

### 5. Staffing and Funding
**Evidence**
- **High risk:**
  - About 1,300 Census employees left through deferred resignation or early retirement, per the employees' union, out of about 13,230 ([AP](https://apnews.com/article/census-bureau-doge-federal-surveys-fe560e377be69e913660a6d90c1ee419); [GovExec](https://www.govexec.com/workforce/2025/07/census-has-long-struggled-staffing-shortages-employees-say-trump-making-it-worse/406840/)). The American Statistical Association estimates a 15% staff loss since FY24 ([ASA](https://www.amstat.org/docs/default-source/amstat-documents/the-nations-data-at-risk-2025/census.pdf)).
  - Leadership has changed: Director Santos resigned in February 2025. In September 2025, career acting director Ron Jarmin was replaced by George Cook, a political appointee ([NPR](https://www.npr.org/2025/09/19/nx-s1-5288846/trump-census-bureau-director-george-cook)). There is still no Senate-confirmed director ([The Federalist, Sept 2026](https://thefederalist.com/2026/09/04/calls-grow-for-trump-to-appoint-director-to-ensure-accurate-2030-census/)).
- **Lower risk on funding:**
  - The FY2026 budget (P.L. 119‑74) gives the Current Surveys account $318.5M, down about 3% from $329M ([CRS IF13105](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IF13105)).
  - Current Economic Statistics, which includes QFR, was requested at a flat $216M.
- I found no staffing figures specific to the QFR branch. The federal staffing tracker you suggested loads its data dynamically, so I could not extract Census figures; it also says it stopped updating December 31, 2025.

**Rating: High Risk.** More than 1,000 staff were lost and leadership was removed. Both meet the rubric's High criteria, even though the budget cut is small.

### 6. Policy
**Evidence**
- **High (strict reading):** DAO 216‑26 (June 2026) is a Commerce Department policy that directly changed QFR's publication method. It followed political criticism of noise-based privacy methods.
- **Moderate:**
